title: 1Password warns of phishing attempts after a hacker gained access to customer information
summary: 1Password said a hacker got access to an employee's company GitHub account and used it to download a "limited amount" of customer information.
content: 1Password, a popular password manager, said an "attacker" gained access to an employee's account information and used it to download some customer data. Illustration by Timon Schneider/SOPA Images/LightRocket via Getty Images 1Password, a password manager platform, said a hacker accessed an employee's GitHub account. The attacker then copied a "limited amount" of customer information, including email addresses. No keys were obtained, but the company warned of phishing attempts. 1Password, a popular password management platform, warned customers of potential phishing attempts following a cybersecurity incident in which an attacker gained access to customer information, including names and email addresses. The company said on Wednesday that an "attacker" accessed an employee's corporate GitHub account and used it to push malicious code to backend services and download a "limited amount of customer account information." 1Password said that the information included names and email addresses, which can be used for phishing attempts by malicious actors. Other data included account and user identifiers, public keys, tokens "present in certain emailed links for invitations, provisioning and account recovery," and other "non-secret account metadata." The downloaded data did not include vaults and items in them, keys that protect customer vaults, account recovery keys, or 1Password apps and browser extensions, the company said. 1Password's incident report said only a subset of customers was affected and that accounts do not need to be updated. A spokesperson for 1Password did not immediately respond to a request for comment. The company said customers should be aware of phishing attempts, including "unexpected emails, texts or calls that mention 1Password, invitations, or account recovery attempts." "1Password will never contact you to ask for your account password or Secret Key," the company said. "Only enter them in the official 1Password app, or on our official website, and only when you've opened the app or typed the address yourself." Read the original article on Business Insider

title: The 10 best movies and TV shows to stream this Thanksgiving weekend
summary: "The Altruists," which tells the story of former cryptocurrency executives Sam Bankman-Fried and Caroline Ellison, is streaming on Netflix.
content: The women of "The Hunting Wives" practice shooting in season two of the Netflix drama. Netflix Netflix's "The Hunting Wives" returns for its second season this week. "The Mosquito Bowl" brings the story of college football players during World War II to the screen. Peacock's "Dig" and Prime Video's "Blade Runner 2099" are among this week's new releases. Whether you're looking for something to watch with the family after Thanksgiving dinner or need to sneak away for some time on your own, streaming services have you covered. Netflix released " The Altruists ," a series about former FTX executives Sam Bankman-Fried and Caroline Ellison and the collapse of the cryptocurrency exchange. The streamer is also bringing back its drama series "The Hunting Wives," and it just added "The Mosquito Bowl," a film based on the true story of college football players who joined the Marines during World War II. Other platforms have plenty to offer, too. Peacock is premiering "Dig," a new comedy starring Amy Poehler and Hugh Laurie, while Prime Video is taking viewers back to the world of "Blade Runner" with "Blade Runner 2099," starring Michelle Yeoh and Hunter Schafer. From comedies and animated adventures to true-crime stories, fantasy, and drama, here are 10 movies and TV shows to stream this Thanksgiving weekend. Netflix's hit drama "The Hunting Wives" returns for season 2 on Thanksgiving Day. Netflix Brittany Snow and Malin Akerman return as Sophie and Margo in the second season of Netflix's drama. Their complicated friendship continues to unravel amid secrets, scandal, and murder in an affluent Texas community. At the start of the new season, the two women are on the outs, but old secrets and new enemies bring them back together. Streaming on: Netflix, November 26 Peter Berg's World War II drama "The Mosquito Bowl" arrived on Netflix just before Thanksgiving. Netflix "The Mosquito Bowl" brings together football and wartime history. Directed by Peter Berg, the movie follows four college football stars who enlist in the US Marines after the attack on Pearl Harbor. The men eventually take part in a football game that becomes a memorable moment in military history. The cast includes Nicholas Galitzine, Bill Skarsgård, Ray Nicholson, and Tom Francis. Streaming on: Netflix, November 25 Michelle Yeoh and Hunter Schafer enter a futuristic world in "Blade Runner 2099." Prime Video The "Blade Runner" universe gets another chapter with this science-fiction series set 50 years after the events of "Blade Runner 2049." Michelle Yeoh stars as Olwen, a dying Replicant, while Hunter Schafer plays Cora, a fugitive who becomes a Blade Runner. The two form an unlikely partnership while searching for a runaway whose secrets could threaten their city. All eight episodes arrive together, giving viewers plenty of time to explore the series over Thanksgiving weekend. Streaming on: Prime Video, November 25 Amy Poehler and Hugh Laurie lead Peacock's new comedy series "Dig." Peacock The comedy follows four women archaeologists working at an excavation site in Greece, where they uncover a rare artifact. Poehler stars as Elise, an ambitious archaeologist hoping to take over the dig from her longtime boss, Neville, played by Laurie. The series also reunites Poehler with Mike Schur, her former "Parks and Recreation" collaborator. All 10 episodes are available to stream now. Streaming on: Peacock (now streaming) Netflix's "The Altruists" follows the scandal that shook the cryptocurrency world. Netflix "The Altruists" tells the story of former cryptocurrency executives Sam Bankman-Fried and Caroline Ellison , whose ambitions to reshape the financial world unraveled amid an $8 billion fraud scandal. The eight-episode series stars Anthony Boyle and Julia Garner and follows the couple's rise in the cryptocurrency industry and the scandal that brought their business empire crashing down. Streaming on: Netflix (now streaming) "Yellowjackets" returns for its fourth and final season on Paramount+. Paramount+ "Yellowjackets" follows the survivors of a plane crash as they try to rebuild their lives after being stranded in the wilderness. "Yellowjackets'" fourth season brings the Emmy-nominated drama to an end, following the women as they face the secrets and consequences of their time in the woods. Streaming on: Paramount+ Premium (season 4 premiered November 20) "Percy Jackson and the Olympians" returns for season 3 on Disney+. Disney+ Walker Scobell stars as Percy Jackson in the third season of the fantasy adventure series. This time, Percy and his friends set out to rescue Annabeth after she's captured by the forces of Kronos. The new season adapts " The Titan's Curse ," the third book in Rick Riordan's bestselling series. Two episodes premiered November 20, with two new episodes arriving each week. Streaming on: Disney+ and Hulu (new episodes weekly) "Steps" puts a different spin on the Cinderella story. Netflix If you've seen enough traditional Cinderella adaptations, Netflix's animated movie "Steps" offers a different perspective on the familiar fairy tale. Ali Wong voices Lilith, Cinderella's so-called evil stepsister, who steals the Fairy Godmother's wand and accidentally turns the kingdom's story upside down. Amanda Seyfried voices Cinderella, and Stephanie Hsu plays her younger stepsister, Margot. Bette Midler plays the Fairy Godmother, while Peter Dinklage also lends his voice. Streaming on: Netflix (now streaming) "Way of the Warrior Kid" stars Chris Pratt as a Navy SEAL helping his nephew find confidence. Apple TV Pratt stars in " Way of the Warrior Kid ," a family adventure about Marc (Jude Hill), a middle schooler struggling with bullying and fitting in. His summer takes a turn when his injured uncle Jake (Pratt), a decorated Navy SEAL, comes to stay with him and his mother. Jake creates a training program to help Marc build confidence. Linda Cardellini also stars as Marc's mother. Streaming on: Apple TV, November 25 "The Magic Faraway Tree" brings a fantasy adventure to the screen. Vertical Entertainment Andrew Garfield and Claire Foy star in "The Magic Faraway Tree," a fantasy adventure about a family that moves to the English countryside and discovers a magical tree near their new home. Their children soon meet the tree's unusual residents and are transported to fantastical lands. The film is based on Enid Blyton's popular children's book series and also stars Nicola Coughlan and Rebecca Ferguson. Streaming on: HBO Max, November 27 Read the original article on Business Insider

title: Peter Thiel bought a historic Bel Air mansion at auction for nearly $100 million less than its original asking price. See inside.
summary: Billionaire Peter Thiel expanded his luxury real estate portfolio with Casa Encantada, a 40,000-square-foot Bel Air mansion bought at auction. See photos inside.
content: The mansion, nicknamed Casa Encantada, has 60 rooms over 40,000 square feet and overlooks the golf course at the Bel-Air Country Club. Nils Timm Peter Thiel bought the historic Bel Air mansion Casa Encantada at auction for a steep discount. Casa Encantada traded for record-breaking numbers multiple times to magnates like Conrad Hilton. The 40,000-square-foot home is now a part of Peter Thiel's intercontinental real estate portfolio. Billionaire Peter Thiel snapped up a 40,000-square-foot mansion in Bel Air for a steep discount at an auction, but he still paid nine figures for it. Casa Encantada, a mansion once owned by Hilton Hotels magnate Conrad Hilton, has been on the market since 2019; it first debuted with a hefty asking price of $225 million. At that price, it would have been one of the most expensive properties sold in the US — a record currently held by Ken Griffin . The home had suitors like Jeff Bezos , who ultimately bought a place elsewhere . The home's asking price has fluctuated over the years, reaching as high as $250 million in 2023, but the final ask was $170 million in April, according to the property's listing history. The former owner of the home was Karen Winnick, the widow of Gary Winnick, a financier who founded the telecommunications company Global Crossing and died in 2023. Gary used the Bel Air home, as well as a different home in Malibu, as collateral for loans he took out starting in 2020, according to The Wall Street Journal, which also first identified Thiel as the buyer. After the Winnicks defaulted on payments, the home eventually went to auction, where Thiel outbid others and purchased it for $130 million. Casa Encantada is one of many properties in Thiel's US real estate portfolio, which includes a compound in Miami , a mansion in Washington, DC , and a property in Maui. But Casa Encantada might be the most historic. See inside Thiel's latest purchase. Casa Encantada was built in 1938, according to Los Angeles County property records. Nils Timm Hilda Boldt Weber, the widow of a glass manufacturer, commissioned architect James E. Dolena to build the estate. Weber was a nurse who married a Midwestern glass bottle manufacturer after nursing him back to health. The death of her husband left her very wealthy, and she spared no expense in building this massive estate. Hotelier Conrad Hilton purchased the home from Weber for $225,000 in 1950. The Huntington Library Hilton lived in Casa Encantada until he died in 1979. The Hilton family then sold the property to Dole Foods CEO and Chairman, billionaire David Murdock, for $12.4 million. The Huntington Library At the time, the deal was a record for the US market. Murdock then sold the home to financier Gary Winnick for $94 million. picture of the home from 1939 The Huntington Library The $94 million price in 2000 was another record. Winnick commissioned architect Peter Marino to help restore the property. The Huntington Library The project took nearly two years and millions of dollars to complete. Today, the mansion spans 40,000 square feet and has 60 rooms, including seven bedrooms and 20 bathrooms. Nils Timm While the Winnicks updated the home for modern living, they kept a classic feel. The main entrance greets guests with a spiral staircase and a grand entry hall with 14-foot ceilings. Nils Timm The basement was once used to house walk-in vaults for silver, fur, and wine. A third of the rooms were once used as dedicated servants' quarters, according to an old listing. Nils Timm Also included in the 60 rooms are multiple living, sitting, and dining rooms. Some are meant for entertaining, but there's also a junior dining room for dinners with fewer guests. Almost every room has a view of the Pacific Ocean and nearby mountains. Nils Timm The property also overlooks the golf course at the Bel-Air Country Club. Casa Encantada's exterior is just as elaborate as its interior. Nils Timm The grounds were designed by landscape architect Benjamin Purdy. The grounds feature formal rose gardens, a vegetable and herb garden, and a tropical botanical garden. Nils Timm There's also a tennis court with a viewing pavilion. The backyard has a tiled, 60-foot pool and views of Bel Air below. Nils Timm There is also an outdoor kitchen near the pool. Thiel bought the historic home at a reasonable price. Nils Timm The Journal reported that the auction started with bids at $125 million, increasing in $1 million increments before it was sold to Thiel for $130 million. Open-air auctions have previously resulted in anticlimactic outcomes; for example, in 2019, a lot in Beverly Hills once listed at $1 billion, sold for $100,000. Thiel is buying property in all corners of the world. Nils Timm In addition to his domestic purchases, Thiel recently bought property in Argentina and New Zealand . title: Dario Amodei accuses rival AI CEOs of ‘vibes-based commercial and political positioning’
summary: The Anthropic CEO said that suggestions that he supports handing over political governance to AI is "absurd."
content: Dario Amodei, the Anthropic CEO, pushed back against claims that he wants AI to govern society. Michael Nagle/Bloomberg via Getty Images Dario Amodei accused rival AI CEOs of paying lip service to human control over AI. The Anthropic CEO pushed back against claims that he wants AI to govern society. Amodei said AI companies are largely aligned on which tasks could be automated. Dario Amodei said Wednesday that humans should keep control of political decisions, even as AI takes on more complex tasks, from driving cars to writing software. In a lengthy post on X on Wednesday, the Anthropic CEO said that rival AI executives are paying lip service to human control over AI while continuing to release products that increasingly automate human tasks. “What is happening is that there’s a sort of vibes-based commercial and political positioning that some AI CEOs are engaging in, where they repeat slogans like ‘human control and agency,’ or ‘AI should be just a tool,’ without actually doing anything different in their products or taking seriously the difficult questions that lie behind these slogans," Amodei wrote. Amodei was responding to an Axios report that some Anthropic employees favor handing certain decisions to superintelligent AI. The report cited his past remarks and noted that rival executives had defended human control without naming Anthropic. Among the examples Axios cited were some of Amodei's past comments in a February interview with The New York Times about how much control people should retain as AI systems become more capable. "I would argue that in many cases, we do want to stay in charge," Amodei told NYT journalist Ross Douthat in a video interview. "That's a choice we want to make, even in some cases when we think the humans, on average, make kind of worse decisions." Amodei said there were safety-critical cases where handing a task over to AI could make sense, but cautioned that society could only adapt so fast. On Wednesday, Amodei called it "absurd" to suggest he wants humans to surrender their free will to AI. He separately said handing political control to AI was a "terrible idea." “This is not AI ‘running the world,’ but AI driving a car, designing a cancer drug, or writing software end-to-end,” Amodei wrote. "Here, my view is mixed. AI doing more complete or larger tasks is economically valuable and can drive important advances in software, medicine, transportation, energy, etc. It is clearly desirable in many cases and will save a lot of lives.” “I don't think that other AI leaders or AI companies have significantly different views from me on whether specific tasks should be automated,” Amodei said, adding that companies across the industry are rolling out increasingly sophisticated AI models . Amodei, however, said there is a caveat to AI automation: some AI deployments might need to slow or stop if they risk serious job disruption. "In some contexts, using AI in too end-to-end a manner may be a cause of serious job disruption ," Amodei said, "And it may make sense to slow or even stop some AI deployments to give people more time to adapt." title: Elon Musk and SpaceX pledge a share each to every active Trump account
summary: SpaceX joins a growing number of companies that have decided to invest in Trump Accounts
content: Elon Musk and SpaceX are jumping into Trump Accounts. Kevin Dietsch/Getty Images SpaceX announced it will give one share to every active Trump Account. Elon Musk will personally match the number of shares donated, SpaceX said. SpaceX's COO has separately pledged more than 2 million of the company's shares. SpaceX said Tuesday that it will give one share of its stock to every active Trump Account . Elon Musk, SpaceX's CEO, will also personally match the number of shares donated by the AI and rocket company, SpaceX said. Gwynne Shotwell, SpaceX's president and chief operating officer, also pledged more than 2 million SpaceX shares. "SpaceX is building the infrastructure of the future and working to make life multiplanetary," the company said in a statement. "We believe ownership of the company creating these systems should extend to the next generation of Americans for their long-term benefit." In July, the Trump administration launched Trump Accounts, tax-advantaged investment accounts for children born between 2025 and 2028. Once an account is opened, the US Treasury Department will make a one-time $1,000 contribution. The Treasury Department has said that the accounts are designed to help families build long-term financial security. SpaceX joins a growing number of companies that have decided to invest in Trump Accounts. Dell, Goldman Sachs, Bank of America, Charles Schwab, and BlackRock have also pledged contributions to the accounts. Read the original article on Business Insider

title: Google builds a new toll booth for AI agents. Could Microsoft follow?
summary: Google's new AI agent access limits could raise costs for OpenAI, Anthropic, and other companies building workplace agents.
content: A motorist pays a toll on the Ohio Turnpike in 1955. Seven decades later, Google is building a digital toll booth for AI agents. AP Google imposes new limits and fees on AI agents accessing Gmail, Drive, and Calendar. The charges could raise costs for OpenAI, Anthropic, Meta, and other AI agent developers. Google and Microsoft control the workplace software AI agents need, giving them enormous power. Google is putting up a new toll booth on the road to the AI-powered workplace. The search giant announced new limits on how often AI agents can access Gmail, Google Drive, Calendar, and other popular workplace software. These agents are designed to do work for people, such as searching emails, scouring documents, creating presentations, updating spreadsheets, scheduling meetings, and completing many other tasks across multiple applications. Starting April 1, developers whose agents require more than 5,000 requests per day per Google Workspace product will have to switch to a paid service or face restrictions. (I thought this was another of Google's April Fool's jokes , but I fear it's not). The limit applies to each developer project, not each individual agent. That means a company serving thousands of customers could burn through its free allowance quickly. This could become a significant new expense for companies building AI agents. Toll booths are lucrative Google says the changes are necessary to keep its services reliable and protect customer data. It estimates that more than 99% of active developers will remain within the free limits. As usual, it's about money, too. "The commercial reason (which Google won't admit) is that they can charge extra for higher usage," Himanshu Sharma, a digital analytics consultant at Optimize Smart, wrote on X. And the restrictions raise bigger questions about who controls the emerging AI-agent economy. Microsoft next? Sharma raised another possibility: Other major software companies could follow Google's lead. Microsoft, for example, could impose similar charges on independent AI agents accessing Outlook, Word, Excel, and other workplace applications. That could give Microsoft an opportunity to favor its own Copilot AI agents, potentially allowing them to operate without the same restrictions or charges. Google faces a similar question with Gemini, its own AI assistant. Business Insider asked Google whether its own AI agents will face the new limits and charges or be exempt. The company has not yet responded. I also asked Microsoft whether it's considering similar rate limits and charges on AI agents, and whether its Copilot service would be exempt. It didn't immediately respond on Wednesday. Charging for agent access The implications extend well beyond Google. Essentially, any company that's built an AI agent, including OpenAI, Anthropic, and Meta, will have to adjust. Meta's Muse attracted more than 10 million users in the US and Canada within weeks of its September launch. OpenAI has introduced its own always-on assistants called Dots , Anthropic has unveiled Claude Duet , and startups like Instinct are racing to build agents that can perform tasks across multiple applications. AI agents like these promise to transform how people work by operating software on their behalf. But many of the most useful applications belong to a handful of technology giants. Those companies now have an opportunity to charge other AI businesses for access. The companies building the future of AI agents are about to discover that someone else owns the digital toll roads. title: A historian says AI solved a 200-year-old mystery in just 22 minutes
summary: Historian Mark Humphries asked GPT-6.2 Astra to find the author of an anonymous 1808 sketchbook. It found a match in 22 minutes, he said.
content: Mark Humphries asked GPT-6.2 Astra to track down the authorship of a sketchbook held at Yale's Beinecke Libary. Enzo Figueres/Getty Images Historian Mark Humphries asked GPT-6.2 Astra to find the author of an anonymous 1808 sketchbook. It found a match in 22 minutes, he said. "What I'm trying to do is point out a thing that the models are capable of doing," he told Business Insider. AI is already solving the great mysteries of mathematics . History could be next. Mark Humphries said that he used OpenAI's tools to find the origins of an anonymous sketchbook dating back to 1808. Better yet, he said it took the AI tool almost no time: 22 minutes. Humphries is a professor of history at Wilfrid Laurier University in Waterloo, Ontario. He's studied the fur trade since the pandemic and has long been interested in an unnamed travel sketchbook held at Yale's Beinecke Rare Book and Manuscript Library . The problem: the sketchbook had some captions, few dates, and charted a path that thousands of travelers took. Humphries is in a community of OpenAI users that gets early access to models for testing. So, he pointed GPT-6.2 Astra at the sketchbook's digital rendering, cranked it up to Ultra on goal mode, and asked it to find the origins. The AI model used primary sources, such as a fur trader's dinner diary and a club's meeting minutes, to narrow down who could be in the sketchbook's locations. Eventually, it identified one man: Louis-Guy-Charles-Guillaume de Rohan-Chabot, vicomte de Chabot. A human could do the same investigation, Humphries told Business Insider in a Wednesday phone call. But the documents GPT-6.2 Astra considered named hundreds of people, all of whom would need to be checked. That would make the process time-consuming, he said. "Are you going to devote the years and years to doing that?" he asked. "The answer is probably no." The AI also gave Humphries a path to prove its conclusion himself. Deep in a historian's Ph.D. dissertation, it found a reference to a diary Chabot kept, which he could order as microfilm copies . Humphries found the handwriting of the diary and the sketchbook to look identical. It was interesting, sure, but not conclusive. "I'm not a handwriting expert," Humphries said. Then there were the entries. The diary's dates lined up perfectly with the sketchbook, placing Chabot in "the right places at the right times," Humphries said. And then, what could prove to be the smoking gun: In the diary, Chabot wrote that he made a sketch of Fort St. Joseph, and specified the view that he was looking at. In the sketchbook, there's the sketch of the same landmark with the same view. "That's kind of the X-marks-the-spot kind of thing you don't typically find as a historian," he said. How historians are feeling about AI Mathematicians have had an emotional response to the rise of AI in their field. They hurled insults at an Anthropic staffer over a joke in a proof. Steven Strogatz wept on "The Daily." Comparatively, the historians have been fairly chill. They asked questions about Humphries' process and joked about the similarity of Chabot to "chatbot." A librarian at Yale that Humphries contacted received the finding warmly, though they've yet to do anything with the information, Humphries said. (Yale didn't respond to a request for comment from Business Insider.) "I'm much more ambivalent toward the technology than people think I am," Humphries said. Mark Humphries Of course, the authorship of a niche sketchbook doesn't have the same implication as the Riemann Hypothesis . And some historians pointed out what Humphries himself said: that a human could do the same thing. The biggest names in AI clearly see Humphries' finding as a win. OpenAI president Greg Brockman reposted him, celebrating the model's solution to a "significant historical mystery." Tech workers flooded his X comments with congratulations or statements of amazement. For his part, Humphries doesn't think AI is equipped to do everything in history. "I'm much more ambivalent toward the technology than people think I am," he said. He doesn't use AI for writing, for example. His goal, then, is to make sure historians know what they're getting into. As math goes through what some call a "crisis," Humphries said, historians should be clear about just what AI is good at. "There are real limitations to the technology," he said. "What I'm trying to do is point out a thing that the models are capable of doing." Read the original article on Business Insider

title: 8 ways to be a good houseguest, according to etiquette experts
summary: Etiquette experts shared ways to be a good houseguest, like keeping shared spaces tidy and coming prepared with your own toiletries.
content: Business Insider asked etiquette experts to share some ways to be a good houseguest. fizkes/Shutterstock Business insider asked etiquette experts about how to be a good guest in someone's home. The pros said tidying up the kitchen and your sleeping space are non-negotiables. Cooking, buying groceries, and giving a gift to your host are kind gestures of gratitude. Whether you're visiting for a night or planning an extended stay for the holidays, someone else's home is not the place to disregard manners. That's why Business Insider asked two etiquette experts for their best advice on being a great houseguest. Here's what they said. Make sure the host is aware of your expected arrival time. wichayada suwanachun/Shutterstock Pamela Eyring, owner of The Protocol School of Washington , told BI that being a great guest in someone's home starts with clear communication. "Be clear and prompt about your arrival time and quickly communicate an updated schedule if you are running late," Eyring told BI. Your host is likely preparing for your arrival — cleaning, cooking, or adjusting their schedule. Keeping them informed on when they can expect you helps prevent stress and shows you value their hospitality. Show gratitude by bringing a gift for your host. BearFotos/Shutterstock Additionally, Eyring said it's always a nice gesture to bring a gift for your host. If you're not sure what they like, she suggests choosing something that appeals to all, like flowers, sweets, or a meal. Be mindful of the tone you set for the visit. Pixel-Shot/Shutterstock It's no secret that travel doesn't always go as planned. But according to business etiquette expert and leadership consultant Sheree Bryant Sekou , bringing a negative attitude and energy to your host's home can impact the duration of your stay. "How you start a trip can affect how it ends, so to the best of your ability, shake off any bad vibes so you can be a fully present, enjoyable, and happy guest," she told BI. Come prepared with your own toiletries and anything else you need to feel comfortable. New Africa/Shutterstock When staying in someone else's home, Sekou said it's polite to come prepared with your own toiletries, personal hygiene products, and anything else you need to feel comfortable during your stay. This way, the host doesn't feel like they have to provide everything for you. For example, if you're particular about your sleep setup, Eyring suggests bringing your own pillow. If you're a light sleeper, bringing earplugs can be a good idea. Overall, planning for your own comfort shows thoughtfulness and helps ensure a smoother stay. Always make your bed in the morning. Pixel-Shot/Shutterstock Whether you're sleeping on the sofa or in a bedroom, it's respectful to clean up the space after you wake up every morning. "Always make ‌your bed when staying in someone else's home. That includes arranging pillows as you've seen them before," Sekou told BI. If your sleeping arrangement is fancy, Sekou suggests taking a photo when you arrive so you can try to match it each day. Offer to help with cooking or pay for groceries. Cooking a meal can help make your host's life easier. Jacob Wackerhausen When staying in someone's home, Sekou recommends helping out in the kitchen in a way that best suits your host, whether that's cooking a meal or buying groceries. " Buying groceries lets your host know you appreciate their hospitality and are respectful of their budget," she said. Always clean up after yourself in shared spaces. Drazen Zigic/Shutterstock Sekou said being a considerate houseguest means cleaning up after yourself in shared spaces like the kitchen and bathroom. Regardless of your habits at home, she said it's important to keep things tidy when staying in someone else's house. This means doing the dishes, wiping down counters , and ensuring nothing is left behind. The same principle applies to the bathroom. Sekou recommends a quick once-over before you leave — rinse the tub after a bath, and make sure no hair, toothpaste, or shaving remnants are left behind in the sink. At the end of your stay, check that you grabbed all your belongings. Pranithan Chorruangsak/Shutterstock According to Sekou, part of being a considerate guest is packing efficiently and ensuring you take all your belongings with you when you leave. "If you've left something behind, it puts the onus on the host to get it back to you, especially if it's something valuable," Sekou told BI. This story was originally published on October 21, 2025, and most recently updated on November 25, 2026. Read the original article on Business Insider

title: Jensen Huang’s message to Nvidia: We don’t need a Plan B
summary: The recently reinstated CEO reportedly says he doesn't believe in succession planning. Preparing for change is widely deemed a board's responsibility.
content: Jensen Huang, CEO of Nvidia Evelyn Hockstein/Reuters Upon returning to the helm at Nvidia, CEO Jensen Huang reportedly said he doesn't believe in succession planning. Governance advisors argue that the chipmaker's board has a responsibility to plan for life after Huang. They also say the company's unusually flat leadership structure makes grooming an heir highly challenging. Extending human life is a popular pursuit in Silicon Valley. At Nvidia, Jensen Huang appears to have little interest in planning for the inevitable. A day after being reinstated as CEO on Monday, Huang reportedly told colleagues he didn't "believe in succession planning ," because it would suggest some executives were more important than others. The idea is consistent with the unusually flat structure at the top of Nvidia — yet also remarkable given the company's recent leadership upheaval. "If the CEO is hit by the proverbial bus, somebody has to be in charge," said Umesh Ramakrishnan, cofounder and chief strategy officer at the executive search firm Kingsley Gate. Assuming Huang is as mortal as the rest of us, Nvidia will eventually need a new leader . While he may not believe in succession planning, experts in corporate governance say it's the board's responsibility to prepare for a future without him. "Life goes on beyond one individual, and when a board is so wedded to one individual, they're making a terrible mistake," said Charles Elson, founding director of the Weinberg Center for Corporate Governance at the University of Delaware. Avoiding a lame duck On Wednesday, S&P Global Ratings placed Nvidia's AA credit rating on watch for a possible downgrade, citing concerns about its management and governance . It said a downgrade could come within 90 days if S&P determines governance deficiencies remain. "Weak executive oversight and lack of succession planning have brought questions around the 'key man' risk to the forefront," S&P said. "The departure, then reinstatement of the CEO, does not sufficiently answer our questions regarding board oversight of executive code of conduct." It's not unusual for a company to lack a succession plan . In a 2025 Nasdaq survey of about 700 board members, CEOs, executives, and governance professionals, 21% said their boards didn't have one, while another 16% said they had only an emergency plan. Huang's departure and reinstatement has caused volatility in Nvidia's shares ANGELA WEISS / AFP via Getty Images Companies that do prepare for a leadership change tend to keep their plans quiet to avoid turning the sitting CEO into a lame duck or prompting passed-over contenders to leave, said Ramakrishnan. Boards should get started well before a crisis, he added, by developing two or three serious internal candidates, giving them substantial operating responsibility, and creating incentives for them to stay through a transition. At Nvidia, Huang has around 60 direct reports, an unusual structure he has credited with keeping information flowing and empowering employees. The downside, some leadership advisors say, is that executives who oversee individual pieces of the business may not be prepared to run the whole company. "It's hard to imagine any of those direct reports are able to get the scale, scope, and experience to even be qualified to be the CEO," David Astorino, a senior partner at leadership consulting firm RHR International, previously told Business Insider. 'A house of cards' The decision by Nvidia's board to put Huang back in charge just 11 days after announcing his resignation also suggests its directors are unwilling to challenge him, Elson said. His departure came amid revelations that he had an intimate relationship with a client; concerns raised by US officials that he may have been the target of a foreign intelligence effort; and reports that he had affairs with two employees , including a direct report. "Given what's happened, he really loses all accountability," Elson said of Huang. "I mean, if that didn't get him out, what will?" Nvidia's board said it gave Huang his job back because it was satisfied with his "candor" and that it had received "input from senior levels of the United States government." But Kim Scott, a former Apple and Google executive and cofounder of the leadership-training company Radical Candor, said Nvidia would be vulnerable if it relied too heavily on Huang. "If it's all dependent on him, then it's a house of cards , and it's going to fall down anyway," she said. Huang, for his part, has acknowledged that he won't live forever and suggested that his successor can reshape Nvidia to suit their own leadership style. Earlier this year, he told Garry Tan, CEO of the startup accelerator Y Combinator , that he expected to die on the job. "The next CEO, whatever their personality is, they can figure it out," he said. title: I went to Miss Universe for the first time and found a fandom that won't quit, no matter the number of scandals
summary: Miss Universe 2025 was plagued with scandals that made international headlines. I went to the 2026 pageant and found the fandom was as loyal as ever.
content: Contestants at the Miss Universe 2026 pageant in San Juan, Puerto Rico, on Tuesday. Jaydee Lee/Getty Images After covering pageants since 2019, I finally went to my first Miss Universe pageant. I wanted to see what the atmosphere would be like after last year's scandal-plagued pageant. The fans — who lined up every morning and night to see the pageant queens — are as loyal as ever. It was just after midnight when the pain of my 4.5-inch high heels had become too much to bear. I was standing alongside hundreds of fans who had lined up just to catch a glimpse of the 116 women competing for the title of Miss Universe 2026 . Two hours had passed without a beauty queen in sight. I stole a glance at the shoes of the pageant bloggers next to me. Flat, sensible, arch support — these were veterans. The Miss Universe pageant has been consumed with controversy over the last few years, but its fandom's fierce devotion was still on full display in San Juan, Puerto Rico, where the 75th annual competition took place this month. I spoke to dozens of people while attending the pageant's three main competitions and found that many were unfazed by its scandals. And after the new winner made history by becoming the first mother to take the crown , it seems the organization is hoping to move on as well. Here's what my very first Miss Universe pageant was like. My Miss Universe journey began at the organization's official museum. Anneta Konstantinides/Business Insider After dropping my bags off following a red-eye flight, I dragged myself to Plaza Las Américas to pick up my press pass and check out the official Miss Universe Experience Museum. The museum wasn't in the mall's directory, and there weren't any signs advertising it. The shopkeepers I asked for help had no idea what I was talking about! After nearly an hour of searching — did I mention this is the largest mall in the Caribbean? — I finally found the pop-up museum. Standing at the entrance was the dress Fátima Bosch wore when she won Miss Universe 2025 after a scandal-plagued competition that included a viral shouting match, multiple judges dropping out, and rigging allegations. I was almost surprised the museum would want to remind people of last year's pageant. But after a few days in Puerto Rico, it was clear that Miss Universe's biggest fans were happy to forget about it. Then it was time for the national costume competition, my first Miss Universe event. I was shocked to see so many empty seats. Anneta Konstantinides/Business Insider Of the four rounds of the Miss Universe competition, the national costume contest is always my favorite. Most of the contestants celebrate their countries with over-the-top ensembles that would fit right in at Carnival or a show in Las Vegas. It's pure camp. So I was really surprised that the Coliseo de Puerto Rico felt so empty. Most of the middle section of the stadium — which can fit up to 18,500 people total — was vacant, as were the nosebleeds. But the official stage was really impressive. Anneta Konstantinides/Business Insider This year's Miss Universe stage was designed as a large "X" framed by shimmering steps. Purple, blue, and gold lights flickered as a projection of the pageant's logo slowly twirled in the middle. It was showtime. The announcers fully committed to the tradition of creating a little rhyme for each costume as the contestants walked across the stage. They seemed to get more unhinged as the show went on. "Doesn't get much hotter than the mother of water!" "You will get your wish if you love fish!" "Life sure is great when you look like a gate!" The unsung hero of the night was the man standing behind the judges, cueing the woman. Anneta Konstantinides/Business Insider This man must have logged 10,000 steps as he ran back and forth on the platform, dramatically waving his hands to direct the contestants. His big white gloves and frantic hand movements reminded me of Mickey Mouse in "Fantasia." The contestants managed to navigate their dramatic backpieces and feather headdresses without a single collision, although Miss Turks and Caicos lost one of her lobster antennae. A stagehand quickly jumped up and grabbed it before the next contestant walked by. After the national costume contest, I headed to the official pageant hotel. Anneta Konstantinides/Business Insider Watching the Miss Universe contestants' arrivals and departures at their hotel has become a tradition of the competition, and hundreds turned out for them every night at the San Juan Marriott Resort & Stellaris Casino. Security at the hotel was strict — everyone who entered needed to get a new wristband every morning and night. If the lobby was at capacity and you weren't a guest, you had to wait and watch outside, even if you were a family member. The pageant bloggers knew the drill and were always the first people there, setting up shop behind the barricade with their ring lights and selfie sticks. The first ones to arrive and the last to leave, these pageant superfans were working on almost the exact same schedule as the contestants. Many of them were livestreaming the entire time. I peeked at one man's camera and saw that 2,000 people were tuning in. "I'm barely eating, I'm barely sleeping, but I know it's worth it," one blogger said. He planned to get to the hotel at 6:45 a.m. the next day in case the women left early. After about an hour, the contestants began to arrive. Some contestants hammed it up for the camera as the bloggers begged them to twirl, others walked by with a quick wave. None of the women were allowed to stop and say hi to their family or give interviews. A security guard stopped Miss Cabo Verde from giving her man a kiss, while Miss Ukraine's family climbed on chairs to wave their flags and catch a glimpse. I returned to the hotel the next morning, where I had a chance to chat with some of the contestants' family members. Anneta Konstantinides/Business Insider I've now covered five different pageants. Speaking to the contestants' relatives is always my favorite part of the gig. You only get to see the women onstage for a few minutes. When you talk to their family members, you learn the whole story behind them. Clarine and Morena Gomberts and Shanoulle Biker are the aunts and godmother of Miss Curaçao Bianty Rojer-Gomperts. They told me how Rojer-Gomperts had put her career on hold to become the sole caregiver for her mother, who is now bedridden with severe Alzheimer's. One aunt had traveled 21 hours across three flights to see her compete. "It's very emotional," they told me. "She did it all for her mother." Many family members were being introduced to the culture of pageantry for the first time. Anneta Konstantinides/Business Insider "This world is really crazy, I had no idea," Miss Ireland's sister told me. "It's so intense how many fans come here. Even yesterday, we couldn't get in. We had to wait outside." There were also pageant veterans waiting to see the contestants, including MonaLisa Parayno, who told me she was attending her third Miss Universe but "almost didn't want to come" after last year's controversies. "I was a little bit disheartened, but it's about the experience," she said. "It's about the girls that we want to support, regardless of the rumors out there." As the fans waited for the contestants, they began hyping up each other's countries. Anneta Konstantinides/Business Insider There was something very sweet about watching the different groups support each other. Someone would spot a different flag and start a new chant, giving each country their moment. "Australia! Brazil! Cuba! Nicaragua!" The hotel lobby filled with cheers as the contestants began to arrive, almost all of them dressed in evening gowns and full faces of make-up at 10 a.m. I only spotted one queen in sweats. A dad ran behind the crowd of fans, yelling his daughter's name and waving goodbye like she was about to catch a flight. A mother turned around and put her fingers in her ears, overwhelmed by the sound. When the crowd began to disperse, we realized Miss Haiti and Miss Romania had been left behind. Anneta Konstantinides/Business Insider I spotted the two contestants as I walked outside the hotel, where I also ran into a very stressed-out hotel guest who clearly hadn't been there for the pageant. "I almost missed my flight, I've been waiting 45 minutes to leave," I overheard the tourist tell another guest as she wheeled her suitcase to a waiting cab. That night was the preliminary competition, which attracted a much bigger audience. Anneta Konstantinides/Business Insider There were huge lines to get inside the stadium, and the middle section was mostly occupied. Since the 100-plus contestants are cut to a top 30 at the beginning of finals, the preliminary competition is the only chance for many family members to watch them compete in the swimsuit and evening gown rounds. The crowd was deafening when Miss Puerto Rico first appeared. Anneta Konstantinides/Business Insider I've always heard that Miss Universe fans bring a legendary energy to the pageant, but I didn't really understand it until I saw how hard they could cheer for their hometown queen. The cheers and applause completely drowned out the hosts as they introduced Jennifer Barreto. We tracked the voice decibel to see just how loud the crowd could go. It maxed out at 103 during preliminaries. On finals night, it went to 107. The three-hour-long preliminary was my least favorite event of the week. Anneta Konstantinides/Business Insider I've covered a few pageant preliminaries, so I knew what to expect. But the arena seats made it hard to see the details of the contestants' dresses — always the best part of the evening gown round— and the air conditioning was turned up to full blast. The couple in front of me was so cold, they huddled underneath a black zip-up jacket. "It's so BORING," their young daughter cried. "It's almost done, don't worry," her mother replied. After it wrapped, I returned to the nightly campout at the official pageant hotel. Anneta Konstantinides/Business Insider As we waited for the pageant queens to arrive, I spoke with Ernest Batac, who has traveled to every single Miss Universe since 2012. When I asked him how much he had spent on the pageant, he said he had no idea. It was priceless for the community he had found among fellow fans. "I work hard and then I play hard," he said. "It's all about reuniting with my friends." After an hour and a half, my feet could no longer bear it. At midnight, I hobbled back to my hotel for a dinner of popcorn like a millennial Cinderella. I learned the next morning that the pageant fans had waited until nearly 1 a.m. to greet their queens. It was finally time for finals! And some big changes were made following last year's issues. Anneta Konstantinides/Business Insider It has been the norm over the last decade for the Miss Universe Organization to announce the judges well in advance of the competition. But after multiple people dropped out in 2025, they kept this year's judges a secret until the night before the final. The accounting firm that oversaw the votes was also given a shoutout at the beginning and end of the show, something I didn't see at Miss Universe 2024 or 2025. After last year's competition, judge Natalie Glebova (who was Miss Universe 2005) posted on Instagram that she would not participate again until an auditor returned to the competition. The arena was nearly sold out, and the production looked impressive and expensive. Anneta Konstantinides/Business Insider My one complaint was that the stadium had very small screens. I could barely spot the dancing flowers, which my editor said were giving "demogorgons from 'Stranger Things,'" from my nosebleed seat. As I strained to see below, I remembered watching the dancing trees from the Super Bowl stands during Bad Bunny's Halftime show . Puerto Rico really loves some jazzy shrubbery! At the end of the night, a historic winner was crowned the new Miss Universe. Barreto is the first married woman and mother to win Miss Universe. Jaydee Lee/Getty Images The arena absolutely exploded when Barreto's name was called. She was bringing the crown home, and she'd be the first married woman and mother to wear it in the pageant's 75-year history. Barreto had defied the words of former Miss Universe CEO Anne Jakrajutatip , who once told her staff that diverse contestants — including married women and mothers — "can compete, but they can't win." (She later denied that she was talking about the pageant). As I walked out of the stadium, the Puerto Rican fans led a chant of "Olé, Olé, Olé," and I contemplated the future of Miss Universe. Anneta Konstantinides/Business Insider Pageants are no longer on broadcast TV or cable. They've lost the millions of viewers, the promise of instant fame. And still the brand endures — why? Miss Universe is still the biggest pageant in the world, and its crown means something different to everyone. For contestants, it could be a childhood dream, or maybe a stepping stone to a different life. Miss Switzerland's family, who I sat next to during the final, told me that one day she just decided to quit her 9 to 5 and apply. For the big pageant countries, there's still massive popularity. For the small island nations, it's a chance to boost tourism and get their name on a global stage, Derri Lee — the national director of Miss Cayman Islands — told me. And for the fans, it's all about pride and connection. For now, that seems to be enough. Read the original article on Business Insider

title: See how Jensen Huang's fortune compares with the richest Americans in history
summary: See how some of the most notable tech CEOs' fortunes compares with 28 of America's richest people ever.
content: Standard Oil founder John D. Rockefeller has long been considered the wealthiest man in America's history, but Elon Musk is now wealthier, and tech CEOs like Jensen Huang don't fall far behind. General Photographic Agency/Getty Images / ALLISON ROBBERT/AFP via Getty Images/Sean Gallup/Getty Images America has more billionaires than ever, led by tech executives like Jensen Huang and Elon Musk. Figures such as John D. Rockefeller and Andrew Carnegie were known as the richest men of their time. Adjusting their historical fortunes for inflation, many still rank among the wealthiest today. America has never had as many billionaires as it does now — and the number is only growing. From multibillion-dollar IPOs to dominance in the production of specialized chips, some of today's most notable tech company leaders, like Nvidia's Jensen Huang , have built fortunes for the history books. While the scale of tech CEOs' fortunes is unprecedented by all measures, it also raises the question of how historic figures, widely considered America's richest, such as Gilded Age industrialists , compare with today's richest people. That is to say: Who are the richest Americans of all time? In many historical calculations of net worth, individual fortunes weren't measured in isolation; instead, they were compared to the US GDP at the time. When the US economy was much smaller than it is today, the wealthiest families and individuals carried more weight in the economy than others during more prosperous times. One of the richest Americans of all time is widely considered to be John D. Rockefeller, founder of Standard Oil, whose wealth, at its peak in 1937, was equal to 1.5% of the country's GDP. His estimated net worth would be around $512.7 billion today, when adjusted for inflation. Elon Musk's current wealth, however, has far eclipsed Rockefeller's. To identify some of the richest Americans of all time, we consulted Forbes' 2007 list of history's wealthiest figures , based on estimates by economist Peter Bernstein . It calculated individuals' wealth at their peak and compared it to the country's GDP at the time to convert it to 2006 dollars. This was then adjusted to today's dollars using the US Bureau of Labor Statistics' inflation calculator . For living individuals, we cited Forbes' estimated net worths as of November 25, 2026. While estimates of historical wealth may not be perfect, they help paint a picture of the wealth enjoyed by some of America's most notable business figures and put it in context with today's billionaires. title: Student-loan borrowers are being notified they’re ineligible for their income-based payments
summary: Student-loan borrowers received notices that they have 90 days to switch off their income-based repayment plan or face higher payments.
content: New notices are going out to student-loan borrowers telling them they're ineligible for their income-based repayment plan. Robyn Beck / AFP via Getty Images The Education Department said it "discovered" some student-loan borrowers are ineligible for an income-based repayment plan. Borrowers received a notice giving them 90 days to transition to a new plan or be placed in a standard plan. Some borrowers said they're concerned the switch could jeopardize their loan forgiveness progress. Some student-loan borrowers got a surprise notice days before Thanksgiving: they may no longer pay off their balances under a more generous version of the income-based repayment plan. An Education Department spokesperson confirmed to Business Insider that a group of student-loan borrowers was enrolled in its newer income-based repayment plan when they were only eligible for an older version. Borrowers with loans disbursed before July 2014 qualify for plans paying 15% of their discretionary income, with loan forgiveness after 25 years. The department said an error led to fewer than 0.1% of borrowers being mistakenly enrolled in a newer, more generous IBR plan, which carries payments of 10% of their discretionary income and forgiveness after 20 years. Only borrowers with loan disbursements on or after July 1, 2014, are eligible for that plan. The department did not comment on the cause of the error and said that affected borrowers can apply for an eligible plan at studentaid.gov. The notice, viewed by Business Insider, said that the Education Department "has discovered that some borrowers were enrolled in the Income-Based Repayment (IBR) Plan for which they were not eligible." MOHELA, a student-loan servicer, said in the notice that the department directed it to remove all ineligible borrowers from the IBR plan. The notice gave borrowers 90 days to select a new plan. If they do not select a plan within that timeframe, MOHELA said it would place borrowers in the standard or tiered repayment plans, which typically give borrowers the most expensive monthly payments. Borrowers who received the notice said they hoped it was an error, given they had been making payments on the plan for months or years. One borrower said she has a few payments to go on the Public Service Loan Forgiveness program, which forgives student debt for government and nonprofit workers after 10 years. The payments she was making under IBR were affordable and allowed her to make progress on her PSLF timeline, and she's worried that switching off the plan would jeopardize that. The department spokesperson said that switching plans should not directly affect PSLF progress. These notices are similar to the ones borrowers enrolled in the Biden-era SAVE plan have received. The Trump administration eliminated SAVE, which allowed for cheaper payments and a shorter timeline to debt relief. Beginning in July, enrolled borrowers received notices with a 90-day timeframe to transition off SAVE or be placed in a standard plan. However, borrowers who reached their 90 days then received an additional 30-day "final notice" to switch plans, and those who have surpassed the extra month are still waiting to be switched. The department has not commented on its timeline for transferring borrowers to the standard plan, and it's unclear if borrowers who received the IBR notice will receive a similar extension. Have a story to share about student loans? Contact this reporter at asheffey@businessinsider.com . Read the original article on Business Insider

title: Terence Tao calls for a transition to ‘math 2.0’ in the wake of AI bombshells
summary: UCLA math phenom Terence Tao is going scorched-earth as AI disrupts his field.
content: UCLA math professor Terence Tao says math needs to undergo a transition. Richard Hartog/Los Angeles Times via Getty Images Terence Tao is going scorched-earth as AI unsettles mathematics. The UCLA professor said incentive structures and academic journals need to change — and quickly. Tao laid out his vision before an Anthropic researcher solved math's most famous problem using AI. Terence Tao is calling for radical change. The UCLA math phenom, viewed by many as a thought leader in the field, recently said mathematicians are living in the past if they think they can maintain their old values and stay relevant in the age of AI . "Math 1.0 is going to have to transition into what I call math 2.0," Tao said at Harvard University last week. To start with, Tao said that solving problems should no longer be the lodestar of mathematical research . Now that AI can tackle dense conjectures more efficiently than humans can, dying on that hill would be foolish, he said. "Further blind optimization of problem-solving alone is now actively harmful to the long-term health of mathematics," his slideshow presentation read. Instead, Tao said mathematicians should focus on subjects that humans already excel at, like explaining what AI-generated solutions actually mean and extrapolating new problems from them. And getting work published in academic journals, once a prestigious accolade for mathematicians, is rapidly losing its value, he said. As submission inboxes become flooded with AI-generated research by less and less capable mathematicians, who in many cases don't even understand what they're submitting, Tao said journals need to rethink their values or lose their importance. "We can't go by just how many papers you have in the top journals anymore," he said, adding that mathematicians should earn clout only if they can explain their research before human inquisitors. Tao laid out his vision to a room full of Harvard mathematicians shortly before the math community was once again rocked by a bombshell AI solution — this time for the most famous open question in all of mathematics. On Friday, a mathematician employed by Anthropic said he cracked the Riemann Hypothesis using Claude. Mathematicians told Business Insider that the breakthrough is a huge deal. Steven Strogatz, a professor at Cornell, called the problem the "white whale" of the field. In an interview on the "Numberphile" podcast last month, Tao said humans working with AI models wouldn't "make progress" on the Riemann Hypothesis before 2050. Still, Tao didn't say that young mathematicians should drop out of their Ph.D. programs and join AI startups. He pointed to Caltech's mathathon , an event organized by students in which participants use AI to find new ways to solve old problems, as a possible way forward for the field. "Despite all the tumult that we have today, the future of math actually is quite bright," he said. Read the original article on Business Insider

title: Former Tesla engineer says AI will create more 'fake jobs' — not mass unemployment
summary: Tejas Bhakta, the founder of Morph and a former Tesla machine learning engineer, said a lot of today's jobs are basically "UBI right now."
content: Employees are worried that AI could replace their jobs. This startup founder thinks it'll create more pointless ones. Matthew Chattle/Future Publishing via Getty Images An AI founder and former Tesla engineer says AI is about to make our paperwork morass worse. Tejas Bhakta said a large part of the internet's jobs are a form of universal basic income. His take on AI's impact on jobs differs from the up-and-down warnings of other Silicon Valley execs. Worried that AI could replace your job ? Tejas Bhakta says he thinks the tech will do the opposite — and add to our pile of useless work. "Some people have this take that we're going to have mass unemployment as a result of this," he said during an interview with MTS Live. "I almost feel the opposite. Like, I think we're going to have more bullshit jobs. Just way more." Bhakta, a former Tesla machine-learning engineer, is now the founder of Morph, an AI-infrastructure startup that was in Y Combinator's Summer 2023 batch. "Basically most jobs are UBI right now." Morph founder @tejasybhakta argues that AI could create even more bullshit jobs rather than lead to mass unemployment: "Most people are in jobs that don't need to exist. These procurement officers that are putting out this paperwork that doesn't need to be done to sign this doc that no one cares about or will ever read. "Basically most jobs are UBI right now. That's sort of the hottest take in there." "Some people have this take that we're gonna have more mass unemployment as a result of this. I almost feel the opposite. I think we're gonna have more bullshit jobs, just way more." "Pre-AGI, 40% of jobs were just not really actually doing anything. In order for that organism to keep surviving, it needs these people to have UBI, otherwise the economy falls apart." "So we'll just have more jobs that are fake jobs while AGI does all the work." @morphllm — MTS (@MTSlive) November 24, 2026 Bhakta's take is different from the roller-coaster warnings coming from other Silicon Valley-based executives. In May 2025, Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei cautioned that AI could wipe out 50% of all entry-level white-collar jobs. AI's top bosses have adjusted their tone in 2026, saying the technology could create a new hiring boom cycle. Bhakta is closer to that boom cycle camp — but with a less rosy tint. His view: Our current economy is filled with "jobs that don't need to exist," including procurement workers generating paperwork "that no one cares about or will ever read." "Basically most jobs are UBI right now," he said, referring to universal basic income. He estimated that 40% of internet jobs are "not actually doing anything." He told Business Insider that his view has been shaped by his time working in Big Tech companies. He said it was common to see teams work on projects that never shipped. "I don't even know if it's an inefficiency," he said. "I think it's just a necessary thing." He added that he isn't arguing that people should be fired. On MTS Live, Bhakta predicted that AI will add to that paperwork morass — but those jobs will continue to serve as an unofficial safety net. "It's almost like the organism of the US, like, in order for that organism to keep surviving, it needs these people to have UBI," he said. "Otherwise, the economy falls apart. And so, we'll just have more jobs that are fake jobs while AGI does all of the work." Read the original article on Business Insider

title: 15 Thanksgiving dishes that don't require an oven
summary: Salads, slow-cooker casseroles, and pasta are all tasty side dishes that don't require an oven.
content: Frying a turkey isn't for the faint of heart. Brett Comer/Houston Chronicle/Getty Images If your oven is full on Thanksgiving or simply out of commission, oven-free recipes can help. Salads, slow-cooker recipes, and pasta are all beloved dishes that don't require an oven. These 15 Thanksgiving dishes are completely oven-free. Whether your oven is crammed full of turkey or it's woefully small, sometimes baking and roasting aren't options on Thanksgiving. This week, people across the country will be making multiple dishes for Thanksgiving dinner , using every available cooking surface and spending an average of 9.6 hours preparing for their guests, according to WalletHub data . Thankfully, there are plenty of Thanksgiving staples or updated versions of the classics that don't require any oven space at all. Even the precious turkey can stay out of that fateful appliance on November 26. Here are the easiest foods you can whip up this Thanksgiving — no oven required. If you want to use your oven for other dishes, you could use a deep fryer for your turkey. Eric Thayer/Reuters Deep-frying a turkey is serious business, one that can end in a fiery disaster, as evidenced in annual police videos . Business Insider previously showed the best way to fry a turkey safely. You could also use a slow cooker for the turkey, freeing up oven space. Slow cooker. O2O Creative/Getty Images Kendra Bailey Morris, author of "The Southern Slow Cooker," previously told Business Insider that a whole turkey likely won't fit in a slow cooker, but a 3- or 4-pound turkey breast can. "The beauty of the slow cooker is that it is inherently self-basting," she said. "Slow cookers create a very moist environment with the condensation from the cooking process often rising to the top of the slow cooker and then dripping back down onto the meat, which helps to keep things moist." She also suggested injecting some fat, such as a herb butter, back into the turkey breast, since the meat is lean. If your oven is full, you can leave soup simmering on the stove or in a slow cooker. Pumpkin soup. Cris Cantón/Getty Images As part of Business Insider's ongoing taste-test series, we've tried the best canned chicken noodle soups , which could be part of a Thanksgiving spread, especially on a budget. Soups or stews that use a slow cooker could be another option for a cold day. Business Insider's food reporter Erin McDowell recommends these three slow-cooker recipes from Martha Stewart . Mashed potatoes can be made from a mix or in the slow cooker. AP Photo/Larry Crowe Instant mashed potatoes might be polarizing, but they are extremely simple. Alternatively, you can make delicious, creamy mashed potatoes in a slow cooker . "Mashed potatoes are great in the slow cooker, though it does take a bit of time for the potatoes to soften, so plan ahead," Sarah Olson , the chef behind The Magical Slow Cooker website, told McDowell. Green-bean casserole is another staple at the Thanksgiving table. Green bean casserole. LauriPatterson/Getty Images Olson has a slow-cooker recipe for green-bean casserole on The Magical Slow Cooker. There are other methods, too — check out this skillet green-bean casserole or this microwave version. Spinach casserole can also be made in your slow cooker. Spinach casserole. Arisara_Tongdonnoi/Getty Images Give this slow-cooker spinach casserole recipe a go. Everyone's favorite pasta dish, mac and cheese, only requires a pot and a stove — or a slow cooker. Mac and cheese. DronG/Getty Images Whether you're making boxed mac and cheese or working from scratch , this side is always a hit. Martha Stewart has recipes for both stovetop and slow-cooker mac and cheese , although we prefer the slow-cooker option. You can make candied yams in an air fryer. Candied yams. bhofack2/Getty Images A Business Insider reporter tried out an air-fryer recipe for candied yams and called it "ridiculously easy." Sweet potatoes are versatile, and all you need to do is microwave them. Robynmac/Getty Images All you need to do to successfully cook a sweet potato is to prick its skin with a fork and throw it in the microwave for 6 to 8 minutes. Cauliflower, or any vegetable really, tastes great pan-fried. Cauliflower. Tatiana Volgutova/Getty Images Here's a recipe for pan-fried cauliflower. Cranberry sauce is a classic Thanksgiving side dish, and all you need to do is open a can. Cranberry sauce. skhoward/Getty Images Find out which grocery-store cranberry sauce was named our favorite. And don't forget: You should always open your cranberry sauce upside down . Stuffing is a Thanksgiving essential that doesn't need to spend time in the oven. Stuffing. Sarah Schmalbruch/Business Insider There's no single recipe for stuffing, and thus no single way to cook it. We previously tried an air-fryer stuffing recipe that was tasty, if not a bit time-consuming. Alternatively, here's an "everything" stuffing recipe that goes in the slow cooker or another that's cooked on the stovetop . Creamed corn turns corn on the cob into an autumnal side dish. Creamed corn. Tom McCorkle for The Washington Post/Getty Images Creamed corn is corn that's scraped off the cob and combined with milk, cream, or even cream cheese, depending on the recipe. Options include a classic creamed-corn recipe , which involves simmering the corn over a stovetop, and a slow-cooker variation . Salad is a tried-and-true side that involves no cooking at all. Fall salad. VeselovaElena/Getty Images Even though Thanksgiving is all about eating until your stomach gives out , that doesn't mean it has to all be unhealthy. We've ranked the healthiest lettuces and leafy greens , and listed everything you need to make your salad as healthy as possible . There are plenty of ways to make cheesecake festive without turning on the oven. Cheesecake. Elena Popova/Getty Images There are many different no-bake recipes out there, but we recommend Martha Stewart's no-bake cheesecake . Read the original article on Business Insider
